newsitem.title: UK: PRESS DIGEST - British business press - Nov 21.
newsitem.headline: PRESS DIGEST - British business press - Nov 21.

text.p: Prepared for Reuters by The Broadcast Monitoring Company
DAILY TELEGRAPH
-- TUNNEL BLAZE COSTS ONE MILLION STG A DAY

The Channel Tunnel fire is costing Eurotunnel one million stg a day in lost revenues. However, the company said that most of these will be bourn by its insurers, led by French UAP and America's Chubb, who will also pay for damages to the tunnel, train, lorries and freight. Eurotunnel and its insurers will be liable to compensate Eurostar, whose daily passenger services have been suspended until further notice.
-- ABBEY AND HAMBROS IN WORLD BANK VENTURE

Hambros Band and the Abbey National have joined forces with Hong Kong banking group Dah Sing Financial Holdings to form an institutional private banking operation. The Hong Kong Wing On Bank will be renamed the DAH Private Bank, whose parent will be DAH Holdings in which Dah Sing, Abbey and Hambros will hold their stakes. A subsidiary bank, DAH Hambro, will be established in Guernsey.
-- ESTATE AGENTS REAP BONUS FROM THE CITY

According to estate agent Savills, City bonuses have helped fuel a 49 percent rise in the price of houses in prime central London locations over the past four years. Savills have noticed a trend that suggests City employees who once would have had a small London flat and house in the country are buying large, family houses in Holland Park and Kensington.
THE TIMES
-- TECS BRACED FOR BUDGET CUT IN YOUTH TRAINING FUNDS

Training and Enterprise Councils are bracing for cuts in funding after it emerged that Chancellor Kenneth Clarke could cut the main government training programme for young people in the budget by up to 20 percent. TEC leaders expect the cuts will provoke strong opposition from business, training providers and the opposition as unemployment among young people remains high.
-- RATE AND BUDGET PRESSURES FOR CLARKE

Chancellor Kenneth Clarke is under pressure from the Bank of England and the City to resist a giveaway budget and consider further increases in interest rates after figures suggesting considerable economic buoyancy. The figures, from the Office of National Statistics, include strong bank and building society lending, a surge in money supply, a new record for car production and a rise in high street spending.
-- BILL GATES GETS THREE PERCENT STAKE IN CHIROSCIENCE

The founder and chairman of Microsoft, Bill Gates, is to take a three percent stake in biotechnology company Chiroscience as part of the group's 120 million dollar acquisition of Darwin Molecular Corp, an American genetic engineering firm. Gates and Microsoft's co-founder, Paul Allen, own 14 percent of Darwin. The all-share deal will give Mr Gates, a director of Darwin, a holding of more than three percent in the Chiroscience equity.
THE GUARDIAN
-- FREEMANS SALE ORDER LEAKS

Chief executive of Sears, Liam Strong, is set to put the group's Freemans mail order operation up for sale in response to institutional pressure for a shake-up at the retailing giant. The business includes One to One and cable TV operation Home Shopper, and City analysts believe it may fetch 500 million stg. Possible buyers are the German mail order group Otto Versand, who have bought Next Directory and N Brown, and Burton, which owns Innovations.
-- CAMPAIGNERS FIND WORKERS ON ONE POUND STG A DAY

A survey by the Greater Manchester Low Pay Unit and the region's citizens' advice bureaux found almost 60 percent of agency workers are paid less than permanent workers in the same workplace. The survey represents a depressing insight into agency work, and poverty campaigners are calling for changes in employment law. The unit says that agency workers could be engaged on contracts that allowed employment agencies to keep almost all the wages of a worker seen as unsatisfactory.
-- IOD DEFUSES MAWHINNEY TORPEDO

The right-wing Institute of Directors have admitted that the economic impact of Labour's windfall tax plan would be insignificant, and a leading shareholder group contradicted claims by Conservative chairman, Brian Mawhinney, that it would hit customers. The IoD is against the tax because it would be hard to compute and to implement, and they believe there are better ways for Labour to fund its employment proposals. However, its position is conciliatory.
THE INDEPENDENT -- NATIONAL POWER PLANS RECS SUPPLY VENTURE

In preparation for the opening of the electricity company to competition in 1998, the country's biggest generator, National Power, is negotiating with three regional electricity companies and a supermarket chain to create a combined electricity supply business. Chief executive Keith Henry said he expects an agreement by next spring. The deal could involve National Power taking a direct equity stake in the supply company or agreeing a long-term alliance to sell electricity to the venture.
-- CABLE AND WIRELESS IN TALKS WITH TELEWEST

In a drive to expand its five billion stg link-up with Mercury and four other UK cable operators, Cable and Wireless is in talks with the cable television operator Telewest. Cable and Wireless is believed to have given itself a year to reduce its 58 percent stake in the Hongkong Telecom division as the colony nears the handover to China. A deal with Telewest could give the group access to more than 600,000 extra phone customers and a potential 4.3 million homes and businesses.
-- 1.5 MILLION STG BALM FOR OUSTED PSION BOSS

The ousted finance director of Psion, Mike Langley, has exercised share options in the company worth 1.5 million stg. He has cashed in stock worth more than 800,000 stg and retains a stake in the company with a value of a further 1.5 million stg. Chairman David Potter described the parting as amicable but felt Psion had outgrown Mr Langley's capability as finance director.
